title: How 787 strangers guessed an ox to within 9 pounds
description:
At a cattle show in Plymouth in 1906, 787 people paid sixpence each to guess an ox's weight. Sort the tickets and take the middle one: 1,207 pounds. The ox weighed 1,198, so the crowd was off by 9 pounds (0.8%), while half the individual tickets missed by more than about 37. Each guess is the weight plus a mistake, too high or too low about equally often, so in the middle the mistakes cancel, and the wild guesses at the ends can't drag the middle the way they drag an average. It only works if people guess on their own. Francis Galton sorted every ticket and published the result in Nature in 1907 ("Vox Populi").

Numbers checked in code: Galton's own centile table (787 tickets, quartiles 1,162 and 1,236, probable error 37 lb), plus 1.5 million simulated guesses showing independent mistakes cancel and copied ones don't. Source: F. Galton, Vox Populi, Nature 75, 450 (1907).

1906 country fair in Plymouth; median 1207 within 1% of 1198; averaging cancels independent errors, not shared ones; social influence makes crowds less accurate (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisdom_of_the_crowd)

Plymouth, 1906. 787 people pay sixpence each to guess an ox's weight.
Collect every ticket and sort them, lightest to heaviest.
Take the one in the middle. The wild guesses at the ends can't move it. 1,207 pounds.
But half the tickets missed by more than 37. So why is the middle so close?
Each guess is the weight plus a mistake. Too high or too low, about as often. In the middle, they cancel.
